description: We are Do-Re-Darren-Mi-Fahh, STEM classmates who love science. Darren wanted to make a game, Elly loves space science, and Jessica, Tatiana and Wei Wei came for the prizes but became just as invested. Our leader shared out tasks and liaised with teachers. Our first 3D survival game didn’t fit the Martian Survival theme, so we switched themes and rebuilt it, keeping the best parts. We disagreed at times, especially on the video, but talked it through. That taught us as much as the project.
summary:
Most students only encounter space in a textbook. Few have stood beside a launch pad or watched a rover drive across another planet. Our project "Fly Me To MARS" gives them the next best thing: a whole mission to Mars that they plan, fly and survive by themselves, in a browser on any phone or laptop.
It starts with $1 billion and an empty spacecraft bay. Players pick a science goal, then choose parts based on real hardware flown to Mars. Every part adds weight, power, data and cost. They choose a launch site and launch window, fly the launch, and steer through entry and landing on a Mars built from NASA's MOLA elevation data. On the surface they keep a crew alive for ten sols, drive a 3D rover to science targets, and sell their samples to earn the cash and power for the flight home.
There are plenty of ways to fail, and none of them are random. Pack an antenna that's too small, and your science never reaches Earth. Overspend on the ground, and you're broke on Mars. Let oxygen, water or power hit zero and it’s game over.
By the end, players will understand why launch windows only open every 26 months, why real mission planners have to balance every trade-off and other small details that affect space travel they would normally not even notice.
details:
Fly Me To MARS is designed for students who would be unlikely to ever get to visit a launch site or mission control. They can develop their own mission to Mars with all decisions affecting the next stage.

Decide the aim of the mission, build your spacecraft using hardware that has flown to Mars, monitor four gauges showing how much lift, money, power and data you have, and plan your launch window. Choose the launching pad from on a spinning globe and head out to Mars. Once on Mars, run your base for 10 sols while oxygen depletes in real time. Drive around on your rover collecting samples on a 3D landscape. Sell these samples and use the power from your base to pay for your return journey. If your mission fails, you can try again but with half the resources, meaning you learn from your mistakes.

When playing the game, you learn that every engineering decision in the rocket building is a compromise. You packed more instruments, which exceeded the budget and failed the weight test; you chose a cheaper launch window, meaning you landed in a sandstorm; and you didn’t include a radio, meaning the science you collected never got to earth. You learn the correct order to do things just by fixing your mistakes. There is also a blitz mode with the quick kit and recommended functions, meaning it can fit into one lesson. Different difficulty modes, scoreboard and second chance mean you can play again.

The entire game is only one HTML file using basic HTML, CSS and JavaScript (Canvas 2D, WebGL and Web Speech API). It can be played on any phone, tablet or desktop without having to download anything or create an account. All statistics are from NASA and are referenced within the game. The AI help is visible on every screen. One economy means everything is connected between Earth and Mars, so everything can be traced back to a design decision. We made sure the game was accurate but still fun to play. Keeping it simple to play and short to fit in a lesson. We used AI in a responsible way, without using any NASA branding or realistic versions.

In a nutshell, by combining space knowledge and casual games, Fly Me To MARS bridges the gap between the fundamental knowledge students have and the experience of being on space missions.
